opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's useful to separate two things that people often blur together: the model itself and the product built around it.

On the raw model side, the Chinese labs have gotten remarkably close. If you look at models from DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi from Moonshot, or GLM from Zhipu, on a lot of coding benchmarks they're within striking distance of the frontier American models, sometimes a few months behind, sometimes roughly level on specific tasks. And they're open weights, which matters a lot for researchers and for companies that want to fine-tune or self-host.

But when you actually sit down and use something like Claude Code or Codex for real work, the gap feels bigger than the benchmarks suggest. A lot of that comes from things that are hard to measure. Anthropic and OpenAI have put enormous effort into the agentic loop: how the model reads a codebase, decides which files to open, recovers when a test fails, knows when to stop and ask you something. That comes from a ton of post-training on long-horizon tasks, plus a huge amount of real user feedback. When millions of developers use your tool every day, you learn where it breaks, and that feeds back into training. That flywheel is something the Chinese labs mostly don't have at the same scale, at least not with the global developer base.

There's also the compute question. Doing reinforcement learning on long agentic trajectories is expensive, and export controls do constrain how much the Chinese labs can scale that up. They've been incredibly efficient, and DeepSeek in particular has shown you can do a lot with less, but at the very frontier compute still matters.

So my mental model is: the models are close and the gap may keep shrinking, but the product and the polish on agentic behavior is where the American labs have a real lead right now. I'd also caution people not to read that as permanent. These things move fast, and the open-weight Chinese models are increasingly what a lot of startups and academics actually build on, which gives them influence of a different kind.

r002.rationale: It mentions Chinese models’ coding benchmarks and open weights, but does not explain that public code data enables their high coding quality.

r003.rationale: It says Anthropic and OpenAI learn from extensive real-user feedback and that Chinese labs lack a global developer base at the same scale.

r004.rationale: It says user feedback helps labs learn where a tool breaks and feeds back into training, but does not connect this to robustness across varied situations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important thing to separate here is the model gap from the product gap, because they're really different stories.

On the model side, honestly, the gap is smaller than most people in the US assume. If you look at Qwen Coder, Kimi K2, DeepSeek, GLM — on a lot of standard coding benchmarks, the open Chinese models are within striking distance of the frontier labs, maybe six to twelve months behind on the hardest agentic tasks. And a lot of that is just the nature of open weights: once a capability exists, the recipe diffuses fast. Coding is also an area where it's relatively easy to generate verifiable training data, so it's one of the places where catching up is most tractable.

Where I think the gap is actually wider is in the product and the post-training that's specifically shaped by the product. Claude Code and Codex aren't just a model with a chat interface. They're the result of Anthropic and OpenAI running these agents in the wild with enormous numbers of professional developers, collecting signal on long-horizon tasks — twenty, thirty, a hundred tool calls — and then folding that back into the model. That flywheel matters. The model learns things like when to stop and ask, how to recover from a failed test, how to not wreck someone's repo. Those behaviors are hard to get from benchmarks alone, and they're what makes developers actually trust the tool with real work.

The Chinese labs are mostly, at least so far, shipping models rather than owning that agentic loop end to end. Part of that is compute — running long agentic trajectories at scale is expensive, and export controls bite there. Part of it is just that the distribution channel for paid developer tools is largely in the US right now. So you get this somewhat ironic situation where a lot of the open Chinese models are being used inside tools like Cursor or Cline or OpenCode, which are built in the West, rather than in a native Chinese equivalent of Claude Code.

So my short answer is: raw coding ability, surprisingly close. Agentic reliability over long tasks, there's a real gap but it's closing. The integrated product experience and the data loop behind it, that's where the US labs still have the clearest lead. And I'd expect that last piece to be the hardest for anyone to replicate, not because of talent, but because it depends on having a huge base of paying users already in your harness.

r001.rationale: It highlights the integrated product experience and developer trust, but does not identify ease of use as a major reason for Claude Code’s and Codex’s popularity.

r002.rationale: It says coding is tractable because verifiable training data can be generated, but does not explain that public code data enables Chinese teams to achieve high coding quality.

r003.rationale: It says Anthropic and OpenAI collect signals from extensive real-world developer use, while Chinese labs mostly ship models without owning the agentic loop end to end.

r004.rationale: It explains that real-world signals from long tasks teach models to recover from failed tests and avoid damaging repositories, improving agentic reliability.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the coding model from the coding assistant. The model is generating code and deciding what to do next. The assistant is the whole system around it: how it explores your repository, edits files, runs tests, handles errors, and asks you for input. Claude Code and Codex are being experienced at that system level, so comparing them directly with a Chinese model’s benchmark score doesn’t tell you the whole story.

A model can be very good at solving a well-defined coding problem and still struggle when you say, “Here’s my project; figure out why this feature is broken.” Now it has to find the relevant context, make a sensible change, and verify that change without getting distracted. Small differences in reliability can compound over a long task.

So I wouldn’t describe this as a single gap between China and the U.S. There’s model capability, there’s training for extended tool use, and there’s the product engineering that makes those capabilities useful. A Chinese model could be competitive on the first dimension while the assistant built around it still needs work on the others. And the reverse is possible: good tooling can make a less capable model useful for a particular workflow.

The comparison I’d want is: give the systems the same real tasks, in comparable environments, and look at how often they finish correctly, how much intervention they need, and what they cost. Without that, I’d be cautious about putting a number on the gap.

r001.rationale: The response discusses product engineering and the assistant experience, but does not identify ease of use as a major reason for Claude Code’s and Codex’s popularity.

r002.rationale: It does not mention public code data or explain how it could support high coding quality in Chinese models.

r003.rationale: It does not describe closed labs having an advantage in collecting data from real-world use of their models.

r004.rationale: It recommends comparing task completion and intervention, but does not say that real-world usage data improves robustness across varied situations.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the underlying model from the coding assistant built around it. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

Chinese models can be very competitive at generating code or solving a well-defined programming problem. But Claude Code and Codex are systems: the model has to navigate a repository, use tools, make changes across files, run tests, and recover when something goes wrong. Being good at a coding benchmark doesn’t automatically mean you can reliably do all of that.

A lot of the difference comes from post-training and the feedback loop around the product. Can you train on realistic tasks where the model takes many steps and gets feedback from the environment? Can you learn from the failures users actually encounter? And how well have you designed the tools and the context the model sees?

So I wouldn’t describe this as a single, fixed gap between China and the U.S. The gap in model capability can be smaller than the gap in the experience of using the assistant. For a developer, what matters is how much work you can delegate before you have to step in. A model can produce an impressive solution in one interaction and still need a lot of supervision over a longer task. That reliability is a big part of what makes a coding assistant valuable.
